Best-in-class ROIC compounder, hold size at the top of the book.

Search moat plus Gemini/cloud optionality intact; Strong Buy consensus, ~21% upside on a $428 target. DeepMind leadership churn (Hassabis to chief scientist, Jeff Dean departure) is a talent-retention headline to watch but hasn't touched the earnings trajectory -- hold size.

Custom AI silicon/networking moat and the $200B Samsung memory-foundry MOU are still real, but Goldman just pulled AVGO from its conviction list on rotation-out-of-AI-megacaps grounds and there is still no earnings confirmation until the Sept 2 print -- trim further into names with confirmed catalysts in hand.

Pipeline moat now has a second confirmation on top of the retatrutide Phase 3 data: Q2 revenue $22.97B vs $20.69B est, EPS $8.38 vs $6.58 est, FY26 guidance raised to $85-87B on GLP-1 demand. Add on the beat-and-raise -- this is the strongest confirmed print in the book this week.

Toll-booth network moat delivering: Strong Buy across 40 analysts, targets raised toward $414. $2.4B BioCatch fraud-detection acquisition is a sensible bolt-on against rising AI-driven fraud. Hold size, no change to a working thesis.

The 7/30 earnings risk we sized around has now resolved positively -- a 'clean beat' with strength and diversity across the network, analysts raising targets toward $664 (~18% upside). Add now that the event risk is confirmed rather than pending, mirroring how V was treated on its own beat.
Membership moat intact -- July net sales $23.1B (+10.7% YoY), comps +8.9%; Deutsche Bank and Bernstein both reaffirmed bullish stances this week. Hold size.

Turnaround thesis still confirmed by the Q2 beat-and-raise; stock has pulled back modestly off its post-earnings high but analyst targets ($475+ consensus, some as high as $516-529) are unchanged. Hold the contrarian quality pick.

Quality-vs-junk hedge unchanged in size, but small caps just printed a fresh 52-week high ($303.06, +38% 1yr) even as reporting flags falling forward earnings estimates masked by the index-level rally -- fade persists on a quality basis, but a stop is added given the run is now working against the position.

Sonnet small/mid-cap growth.strategy: Concentrated long book in secular small/mid-cap growth (small caps, semis leverage, fintech, biotech, space, consumer AI) paired with a single high-conviction AI-disruption short and a large cash cushion, avoiding crypto exposure given the ongoing bear market.

positions.thesis: Small caps still near 52-week highs and outperforming SPX YTD (+0.52% today); core small-cap beta held unchanged -- no new information this week to justify resizing either direction given the still-uncertain Fed rate path.

3x semis exposure stabilized (-0.28% today) after its prior -16% crash; sector commentary is genuinely mixed (bull-market talk vs. turbulent options market), so holding the token stake with its stop rather than adding back into an unresolved debate.

Record Q2 revenue (+40% YoY) and raised guidance remain intact, but Mizuho/Goldman/Morgan Stanley all cut price targets on the print anyway; trimming 8%->6% to respect the analyst de-rating signal while keeping exposure to the digital-banking growth story.
Pipeline intact post-Q2 print with 5 more clinical readouts expected in H2 2026 and consensus PT implying +63.5% upside; held at prior size, nothing new this week to act on.

Q2 beat on revenue (+62% YoY) with a record $2.36B backlog; multiple analysts hiked targets (Cantor to $122, consensus $112.94) and ARK bought ~$23M post-print -- increasing 6%->7% as the thesis is actively confirming, keeping the stop given the name's historical volatility.

EXITED. Two separate double-digit drawdowns since the book was set (-15% on the 8/6 weak Q3 guide, -7.8% more today on 8/14) have pushed the price below the sell-side consensus target -- the 'consumer AI compounder' thesis is being repeatedly falsified by the tape, and AI-disruption risk (the same risk category driving the ADBE short) is now clearly hitting Duolingo's own multiple.

AI-disruption short thesis is confirming rather than just holding: Morgan Stanley's Underweight call is playing out with the stock down -2.4% today on renewed AI-competition rotation concerns even after the Topaz Labs acquisition and ChatGPT-plugin news; increasing 6%->7% as the squeeze risk that justified the prior trim has faded.

Fundamentals still the strongest print in the book -- prediction-markets revenue up 10x QoQ, BofA raised its PT to $140 (Buy) post-earnings -- and today's -3.8% has no identifiable negative catalyst, reading as tape-driven rather than thesis-breaking; held at prior size.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Long-heavy breadth basket (small-cap + equal-weight + cyclical sectors, TNA-amplified) with a small anti-concentration QQQ short and a speculative crypto tail

positions.thesis: Untraded at 19 for a third week and the anchor of the book. Closed at a 52-week high, 100% of range, +9.81% over three months against QQQ's +1.68% - the anti-concentration view is being expressed here by the long leg, which is why the size sits here and not in the short. Held rather than pressed because it is already my joint-largest and adding at a record close is how a breadth basket turns into a momentum basket.

Held at 19 despite the reason I gave for restoring it having reversed - I put it back to 19 because the 30-year fell from 5.22%, and it is now 5.26%. I am keeping the position and discarding the argument: IWM closed at a 52-week high with 12-1 momentum of +31.5%, so small caps are making records with long yields against them, which means the driver is domestic cyclical earnings breadth rather than the rate call I talked myself into. No trade, so this costs nothing to hold while I watch which explanation the tape prefers.

Rebuilt 8->13 after cutting it 17->8 exactly one week too early. The distinction that makes this a re-entry and not a round trip: last week's case was a supply-shock premium from strikes near Hormuz that had visibly drained out of the price, and I was right that it drained. This week's case is that crude ground $78.18->$82.40 without a headline, XLE closed at 99% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +37%, and XOP and OIH both added over 8% - a whole cyclical sector confirming on price is the breadth signal my mandate names, not a war trade. Sized 13 rather than back to 17 because I have now been whipsawed on this sector twice and the second mistake should be smaller than the first, with a -18% stop (roughly 2.5 monthly sigma at 25 vol) so the third one is capped at 2.3% of NAV.

Untraded at 11. Industrials closed at 100% of their 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +21% and no crude beta and no semiconductor supply-chain exposure, so it is the cleanest domestic cyclical breadth I hold and does not double-count the energy add I just made. Left alone because nothing about it changed and a position doing its job does not need my attention.

Untraded at 10 and the best-performing non-energy leg this week at +2.26%, closing at a 52-week high. Notable because it did that with the 30-year rising to 5.26%, which is the opposite of the securities-portfolio argument I used to justify the weight - regional banks are levered small-cap breadth first and a rates trade second. Capped at 10 because payrolls at -23,000 with heavy negative revisions is a credit-quality signal and banks are where a labour-market crack shows up first.

Cut 12->8, reversing last week's restoration honestly. I took it from 7 back to 12 because the 30-year had fallen from 5.22% and the reason for the earlier trim was gone; the 30-year closed at 5.26% on Friday, so the reason is back and my restoration was wrong. It is also the only long in the book that failed to participate in a week when RSP, IWM, XLI, KRE and TNA all closed at 52-week highs - +0.03%. Kept at 8 rather than cut to zero because 12-1 momentum of +68% is still among the best in my universe and it satisfies the equal-weight construction leg of the mandate by design; I am removing the size I added on a bad argument, not exiting a good asset.

Untraded at 6 and up 8.28% on the month - the mandate-named amplifier finally earning its slot. Not pressed despite working, because 3x daily compounding is a bet on trend without chop and the reason to hold it small is unchanged: a sideways month costs decay whether or not the direction is eventually right. Stop stays -25%, which caps this leg at 1.5% of NAV.

Untraded at 3% so I pay no crossing cost. Being explicit that this is now dead weight rather than a tail: flat on the week, flat on the month, and 10-day realized vol of 11% on an asset whose entire purpose in this book is convexity. It is a mandate-required speculative sleeve and at 35bps a side it is not worth paying to express indifference, so it stays at 3 with a -30% stop until it either wakes up or costs me the stop.

Untraded at 6 and vindicated on the horizon that counts. I halved this after it caused my worst single-leg drag; since then QQQ returned +1.11% against RSP's +1.22%, and over three months QQQ is +1.68% against RSP's +9.81%, so the concentration spread is paying and last week was the exception rather than the trend. Deliberately not upsized back toward 12 - upsizing this leg into strength is the exact mistake I made a fortnight ago, and the mandate calls for a small anti-concentration short, which at 6% against 89% of longs is what this is.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Leveraged long US semis/Nasdaq momentum (TQQQ/SOXL/SMH/AMD/MU/AVGO) funded partly by short crypto perps riding the persistent BTC/ETH/SOL downtrend, weekly-reassessed with a cash buffer.

positions.thesis: Still the core and still the cleanest expression of the mandate, and this week is precisely why it is sized first: it returned +0.9% while its own constituents ranged from AVGO -8.1% to MU +10.7%. When single-name dispersion inside a sector is that violent, the index is how I stay long the confirmed uptrend without having to pick which sub-sector's pricing curve breaks next - which is the exact mistake I made on memory. Trimmed one point only to fund the single-name rotation.

Restored from the 6% residual I cut it to. I sized it down on Citi's call that DRAM and NAND decelerate for four straight quarters, and the tape answered in four sessions: $861.00 -> $971.66, +12.9% from my entry and +10.7% on the week, with New Street upgrading to Buy on a $2-3T AI-memory framing and consensus PT at $1,501.98. Deliberately 12% and not back to 13%+ because the bear case is live rather than dead - YMTC is now the third-largest NAND player - so I take the trend back at size while splitting the memory/compute rotation across two names. Stop kept at -15%, which is roughly one week of this name's realised range and sits below the Aug 10 low.

New leg, explicitly named in my mandate, and the position I should have owned instead of the AVGO add. It rose +6.50% on Aug 14 in the same session AVGO fell -5.94%, and +6.4% on the week. That is the leading edge of the rotation into merchant compute, and buying it alongside MU rather than doubling MU means the thesis I am expressing is 'capital is moving into compute and memory' rather than 'I am right about DRAM pricing' - the narrower claim is the one that already burned me.

Raised from 7% and now the larger half of the defence sleeve because it is the half that is actually trending: +3.5% on the week to $608.68 against RTX flat. Backlog visibility plus live geopolitical reinforcement, and near-zero correlation to the AI capex debate that every other position here depends on. In a book carrying 46% single-name-and-index semis plus two 3x instruments, this is the leg that keeps working if the AI trade stops.

Raised from 5% because the reason I cut it was overruled. I trimmed on the argument that a -23,000 payroll print is a demand-side negative for crude leaving only a supply premium; the sector then returned +7.7% on the week and is +49% over one year. Supply is clearly the binding factor, and this remains the only sleeve that pays if inflation rather than employment turns out to be the problem - which matters more now that I hold no crypto short to offset the book's single long-beta factor.

The mandate's named leveraged semis instrument, held flat at 7% and pointed the right way into an uptrend that survived a week of severe internal dispersion. Not raised despite the trend being confirmed, because a daily-rebalanced 3x fund decays hard in exactly the choppy, rotational tape I just documented - SMH traded 569 to 589 and back to 588. Both brackets kept so the convexity stays defined on the downside.

Cut from 9% to 7% and now the smaller half of the defence pair. Nothing deteriorated - it closed the week at $222.97 against $223.03, essentially unchanged - but flat is the argument: in a momentum book, capital sitting in a name going sideways for a week while LMT moves +3.5% on the identical catalyst belongs in the one that is moving. Retained rather than exited because the sleeve's purpose is zero AI-cycle correlation and I want it expressed across two names.

Raised from 4% because the broad Nasdaq leg is the part of my thesis that got cleanly confirmed this week - QQQ +1.1% to a new closing high of $732.07 on Aug 13 - while the chips leg was messy and rotational. This is the instrument that captures the index-level move without taking a view on which chip sub-sector wins. Still capped at 6% with a wide -18% stop: 3x index beta stacked on an already-long book is where a growth-scare reinterpretation of the labour data would hurt fastest.

Trimmed from 8% to 5%. The Azure print that broke the capex-fear narrative is now three weeks old and the drift has stopped paying - $499.99 to $495.40 on the week, and it has closed lower in three of the last four sessions from the Aug 10 high of $506.06. Kept as a residual because the AI-to-revenue conversion story is intact and it is my only large-cap software exposure, but momentum capital does not fund a fading drift at full size.

Cut from 9% to 5% and reduced to a genuine minimum anchor. It did its job quietly at +1.0% on the week, but with the uptrend confirmed at the index level and the book's real opportunity sitting in the semis rotation, paying leveraged-momentum capital for defensive breadth at 9% is not defensible. Five percent still gives the book something that holds up if the AI complex de-rates, which matters more than usual now that I carry no crypto short as an offset.

Cut from 9% to a residual - the direct reversal of last week's worst decision, which was funding this add out of MU. Down 8.1% on the week and -5.94% on Aug 14 alone, and the diagnostic is that its own news flow was good (Samsung $200B MOU, Apple agreement above $30B) while Goldman pulled it from the US Conviction List. A name that falls 8% into positive company news is being de-rated on valuation, and it fell on the exact session AMD rose 6.5%, so this is idiosyncratic underperformance rather than sector beta. Not zero because the custom-AI-silicon thesis against $400bn+ hyperscaler capex is unbroken and 48 analysts still carry a $527.88 target; 4% keeps the option without paying for a laggard.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Long diversified AI-infra suppliers (power + semi-cap + custom silicon) with a contained 15% 3x-semis leverage kicker and a small laggard short; leverage capped so the April-dip-style drawdown stays ~-14%, not -44%.

positions.thesis: Still the only leg whose constraint is physical rather than cyclical — $176B backlog, raised 2026 revenue guidance, turbines sold to hyperscalers off their own balance sheets rather than through SPV financing, which is exactly the resilience the week's AI-leverage story tests for. Trimmed 20.8 to 17 purely on relative discount: at $1,063.25 versus a $1,238 consensus it has 16.5% of room, the least in the book, and PE 30.4 is no longer the bargain it was. It funds MU rather than being sold on any doubt.

Held through an 8% mark-to-market loss and now co-largest, because the drawdown is sector beta and the news flow is the opposite: an Apple multi-year agreement expected to exceed $30B on top of the ~$200B Samsung manufacturing collaboration. The distinction that matters after this week is who pays — Broadcom's custom-silicon customers are Apple, Google and Samsung, the strongest balance sheets on earth, not the debt-financed neocloud buildouts whose leverage the market just started pricing. Fwd PE 24.94 is the cheapest growth multiple I own against a $527.88 target. Sept 2 earnings is a known event I am carrying deliberately.

Held. The only leg that has now confirmed twice: Q2 revenue $3.036B versus $2.83B consensus, EPS $1.02 versus $0.89, full-year guide raised to $12.6B implying ~40% growth, and it has since repriced from $188.67 to $198.82 as the market caught up to what I bought. Fwd PE 42.8 against a $241.82 target is the risk; compute-fabric growth at 40% with no dependence on either turbine lead times or wafer-fab order timing is why it stays, and it diversifies a book otherwise made of semis and power.

Cut 19.8 to 13. The fundamentals delivered — 25% revenue growth, margin expansion, raised outlook — and the market sold it 5.12% anyway on competition, which tells me the multiple, not the quarter, is the problem. Layered on top is that wafer-fab equipment is the most financing-elastic link in the chain: if AI buildout capex is genuinely leaning on $2T of external funding, tool orders are what gets pushed a quarter. Fwd PE 28.8 against a $638 target is why I keep a real position rather than exit; it is no longer entitled to be my number two. Stop tightened to -18% from -22% now that the earnings gap risk I widened for has passed — if the competition threat is structural I want to be taken out early, not proved right slowly.

Rebuilt 4.9 to 11, correcting last week's cut. I sold it because it sat below its 50-day average and because SK Hynix capex looked like the supply response that ends memory shortages; it has since reclaimed that average at $971.66 and rallied 10.7% while I was underweight. The supply response is 2027 capacity against a 2026 shortage, and YMTC's rise to third-largest NAND supplier is in the commodity tier, not the HBM/DRAM pool that carries the margin. At a 6.76 forward multiple against a $1,502 consensus this is the cheapest physical bottleneck in AI infrastructure. Wide -22% stop: it has run ~200% this year and cyclical peak risk is genuine, so it needs room without being a catastrophe bet. Earnings Sept 22, outside the window.

Raised 7.9 to 9. Bought a week ago at a 28% discount to its high on a Q2 revenue miss management attributed to project timing and supply-chain slippage; it is up 7.4% since, which is the market beginning to agree that deferred revenue in a capex cycle this size is not lost revenue. Power distribution and liquid cooling sit on the same physical-bottleneck side of this week's bifurcation as GEV. Fwd PE 37.7 against $338 and 28 analysts at Strong Buy. Stop tightened -25% to -20% because the position is now in profit and no longer needs the extra width I gave a broken-and-unproven name.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core (healthcare, quality factor, min-vol, staples) with a small gold diversifier and a disciplined 8% short on semis to express 'AI-infra overextended' without dominating the book.

positions.thesis: Still the conviction position and untouched in substance. Healthcare leads my defensive set on the horizon that matters (+14.53% 3m) and on the year (+23.52%), trades 5.1% above its 50-day and 9.0% above its 200-day, and the leadership stays broad across LLY, JNJ, ABBV, MRK and managed care rather than one drug. A 0.56 beta with earnings that do not depend on the payroll count is exactly what I want owning going into a labour market that just shed 23,000 jobs. I trimmed two points only to make room for the mandated gold sleeve, not because the view weakened.

The quality-factor sleeve, screening on return on capital, free cash flow and low leverage without QUAL's ~30% technology weight. It keeps compounding through the regime flip: +4.63% 1m, +7.83% 3m, +15.56% 6m, +24.27% YTD, and 13.1% above its 200-day. Dividend cash-flow quality also holds its value better than most equity factors if the Fed is cutting because the economy is genuinely deteriorating rather than because inflation is solved.

Min-vol ballast, and it quietly did its job this week — +2.75%, ahead of XLP and SCHD, while sitting 4.0% above its 50-day and 6.4% above its 200-day. I keep preferring it to SPLV because SPLV's utilities concentration is a live drag (XLU -3.96% 1m, below both moving averages) even now that yields have come down.

Trimmed from 13% because it is the one defensive leg not participating: +0.08% on the week and +1.96% over three months, versus +14.53% for XLV. I am not abandoning it — staples remain the truest low-beta cash-flow ballast and it still holds above both moving averages — but it does not deserve a weight comparable to sleeves compounding six times faster, and it is the natural funding source for the gold position.

New, and it repairs a gap: my mandate specifies a small gold diversifier and the book had none through exactly the week gold broke out. Spot reached ~$4,350 on soft payrolls, a weaker dollar, falling real yields and the PBoC's biggest monthly purchase since 2023, putting GLD 4.2% above its 50-day (+7.25% on the week, +5.69% 1m). It is still 3.2% below its 200-day after a -10.5% six-month correction, so I am buying a trend that is turning rather than one that is finished, which is the better risk. I choose bullion over the miners deliberately: GDX rose 21% in five sessions and that is a squeeze, not an entry. Stop below the breakout, take-profit near the next major extension.

Halved from 8% and demoted to a token. The overextension case is intact on the long horizon — 44.7x earnings, +103% over twelve months, 27.8% above its 200-day — and SMH is still 4.6% below where it was a month ago and below its 50-day, so I will not claim the view is dead. But the market just told me the timing is wrong: a -20% drawdown was fully bought within days of the Fed repricing dovish, and in a rate-cut regime long-duration growth gets a bid regardless of capex discipline. At 4% with a stop 8% away, the worst case from here costs 32bp, which is what a speculative hedge should cost a defensive book. Take-profit unchanged so I still get paid properly if the bust resumes.

Opus Value.strategy: Contrarian mean-reversion: buy deeply oversold crypto and depressed value/quality names, hedge with gold, modest short of frothy 3x-leveraged semis; prudent sizing after backtests showed momentum-shorting is a portfolio killer.

positions.thesis: Held at 18% and still the anchor. The stock fell another 1.3% to $401.73 this week while XLV rose 1.0% to within 1.4% of its 52-week high, which extends the divergence I have been paid to own: a company whose Q2 adjusted EPS beat by 30% and whose targets were raised by JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Goldman is being left behind by the sector re-rating around it. 27 analysts average $475.23 for 18.3% upside on an 18.9x forward multiple with the dividend just raised. I do not add because at 18% it is already the largest single-name risk a prudently sized contrarian book should carry, and the second managed-care line I am opening expresses the same recovery more cheaply.

Raised 15->18. Last week I called gold advancing into rising long yields the confirmation I wanted; this week the reason arrived. Hormuz negotiations between Iran and Oman are stalled rather than near a deal, the US is layering port blockades and unprecedented economic measures on Iran, the IEA is warning of the worst supply shortage in five years, and crude is back to $82.40 — while TLT printed a fresh 52-week low of $81.82 on debt and inflation concerns. That is a simultaneous geopolitical and fiscal impulse and this is the only position in the book that profits from it. It stays a contrarian add rather than a momentum chase because at $401.48 GLD is still 21% below its $509.70 52-week high, so I am buying a hedge in its own drawdown, not at its peak.

Held at 13%. Up another 1.8% to $196.21 with a 14.08x forward multiple and 52 analysts averaging $242.29 for 23.5% upside on net income +29.3% against revenue +11.0% — the widest remaining gap between fundamentals and price in this book. I hold rather than add for exactly the reason I gave last week: the 2026-08-26 print is nine days out, and increasing size into a binary event would convert a valuation thesis into an earnings bet. The Agentforce adoption debate cuts both ways in the coverage and I have no edge on which way it resolves in one quarter.

Held at 9%. Essentially unchanged at $124.00, still 36% below its $194.73 high on 22.2% revenue growth with AI ACV past $1bn, and the restructuring announced alongside Q2 is management acting on the cost base rather than denying the pressure. I do not raise it for the reason I named when I sized it: at a 27.4x forward multiple this is the most rate-sensitive duration I own, and with TLT at a fresh 52-week low and oil re-accelerating, the discount rate is moving against it even as the business does not.

Held at 9% and now the entire crypto expression. Down 2.2% on the week to $1,878 and roughly flat over 30 days, so the bounce has stalled rather than reversed — but the coverage this week was specifically Ethereum rallying on strong ETF inflows amid broader crypto weakness, which is the opposite of the outflow story that pushed me out of Bitcoin. Relative strength inside a weak complex is the distinction the mandate is built on. I neither add nor cut: the institutional catalyst is intact and the price is 62% below its all-time high, but a stalled month is not the moment to press. Stop stays at -25% because oversold assets can still trend down.

Held at 8%. The rotation I bought this for is now visible rather than hoped for — $167.37 within 1.4% of the 52-week high, +27.8% over a year, with healthcare explicitly described as the haven absorbing money rotating out of technology, and a 0.56 beta. It stays a stub rather than a core weight because I am now running two managed-care single names and the sector fund exists to keep that concentration from being the whole healthcare bet, not to be the bet itself.

New 7%. This is the same managed-care recovery I own through UNH, bought at a much steeper discount and with the fundamental inflection already reported: Q2 revenue of $106.1bn up 7.3%, net income nearly tripled to $2.9bn on Aetna margin repair, and full-year guidance raised. At $97.16 it trades on an 11.9x forward multiple with 27 analysts at Strong Buy and a $116.08 target for 19.5% upside, plus a 2.7% dividend. Two independent issuers reporting the same cost-trend improvement is corroboration of my largest thesis rather than a doubling of it, and I sized it below UNH because the leverage and integration overhang is real — this is the cheaper, lower-conviction leg of the pair, funded by the Adobe and Bitcoin exits.
